case_study_insert.main_stem: Clearview Optometry & Eyewear (CVO) is a private limited company in the healthcare retail sector, providing sight tests and designer eyewear from one flagship store, and employing a workforce of 41. Founded in 2012 by Dr Marcus Whitmore, the business operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. CVO plans to invest $780,000 in advanced retinal-scanning diagnostic equipment and a second boutique branch, financed by a $480,000 share issue to existing shareholders and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $232,000 a year, a variable cost of $26.00 a unit and a selling price of $55.00, and currently produces 14,500 units a year, measured in patient consultations and eyewear sales. CVO faces rising appointment waiting times and a shortage of dispensing opticians.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — September 2026: A survey of 420 respondents found that 69% would pay a premium for designer eyewear and 57% of under-30s prefer contact lenses to glasses. Average appointment wait is 12 days. The store conducted 2,150 eye examinations last quarter, and boutique frame sales rose 18% year-on-year. Complaints fell from 15 to 7 per month. A training needs analysis shows 10 of 41 staff need advanced retinal-scanning certification; off-the-job training at the optometry college costs $640 per employee. CVO is piloting recycled acetate frames in its designer range.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Clearview Optometry & Eyewear for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs and weakening consumer confidence. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.40 to $13.16 per hour from April 2026, raising wage costs for retail and reception staff. (3) Imported lens and frame materials have risen 13.8% year-on-year due to currency movements, while consumer spending on premium eyewear grew 5.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: CVO plans to finance its second branch with a share issue to existing shareholders. Explain two advantages for CVO of the share issue instead of taking out a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue to existing shareholders brings in $480,000 with no mandatory repayments and no interest, crucial while the base rate sits at 5.25%. CVO avoids committing its consultation income to a lender, keeps cash for fit-out and stock at the second branch, and pays dividends only if profits allow — a flexible cost of capital while the boutique ramps up.

Point 2: Because existing shareholders subscribe, ownership and control stay within the founding Whitmore family and loyal existing shareholders, with no outsider board seats or lender covenants dictating how the retinal-scanning suite is used. There is no repossession risk over the flagship store or diagnostics kit, the issue signals confidence to staff and suppliers, and it preserves bank loan capacity for contingencies — strengthening the case for a $780,000 organic expansion without bank dependence.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Clearview Optometry & Eyewear and its branch expansion decision.

questions.question_text: CVO is launching its second boutique branch. Consider national television advertising, a social media campaign, or an in-store launch evening with style consultations. Which should CVO choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: Television would announce the second branch to millions and build rapid awareness for the Clearview brand. However, production and airtime costs are unrealistic next to a $780,000 expansion financed by shareholders, and the audience is overwhelmingly outside CVO's retail catchment — the wastage would be severe for a 41-employee independent that wins on service, not scale.

Social media campaign: Targeted content showcasing designer frames and retinal-scanning technology speaks directly to the 69% of respondents willing to pay a premium and the 57% of under-30s who prefer contact lenses, with measurable clicks, appointment bookings and frame-reservation codes. Costs are controllable and results visible within weeks, though conversion depends on frequent, high-quality content and influencer styling partnerships.

In-store launch evening: An evening of style consultations, frame styling and designer previews would convert existing patients and their friends at high rates, deepen loyalty and flatter the boutique experience. However, one evening touches only a few dozen households and generates no sustained awareness ahead of opening; without pre-launch buzz, even the best event underperforms.

Recommendation: CVO should choose the social media campaign as the lead channel. It reaches the premium segment its research identified, is measurable, and builds demand for both the boutique and the clinical suite before doors open. National television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for an independent; the launch evening is rejected as the lead strategy although it works excellently as a closing activation — CVO should use it to convert the social-media audience into opening-week bookings.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CVO with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CVO with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and the launch evening are rejected as the lead channel.

questions.question_text: CVO faces rising appointment waiting times and a shortage of dispensing opticians. Explain two benefits for CVO of its flat organisational structure when managing its team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A flat structure shortens the chain of command between front-of-house, dispensing opticians, clinical optometrists and Dr Marcus Whitmore, so decisions on staffing rotas, stock and appointment triage are made in hours rather than weeks. That responsiveness is exactly what CVO needs to compress the 12-day average wait and absorb demand for the 2,150 examinations conducted last quarter.

Point 2: A flat structure widens spans of control and gives the 41 staff genuine autonomy and visibility of decisions, satisfying esteem needs and encouraging team members to flag clinical issues — for example retinal-scan anomalies — immediately. Faster, freer upward communication improves patient safety and service quality, eases the dispensing-optician shortage as staff feel heard and valued, and supports the boutique's consultative selling culture.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CVO's waiting times, staffing shortage and flagship boutique.

questions.question_text: CVO must certify staff to operate the new retinal-scanning equipment. Consider on-the-job training by the equipment supplier or off-the-job certification at the optometry college. Which should CVO choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training by the supplier: Supplier-led familiarisation is delivered on CVO's own machines, covers exactly the retinal-scanning workflow used in store, costs nothing beyond the equipment purchase agreement, and keeps staff earning while they learn. It protects the 2,150 examinations a quarter. Its limits: it is not a recognised qualification, depth of clinical interpretation is variable, and it leaves auditors without independent evidence of competence for a regulated diagnostic procedure.

Off-the-job training at the optometry college: The college course gives structured, assessed training and a recognised certification for the 10 staff flagged in the needs analysis; 10 x $640 = $6,400, trivial beside a $780,000 expansion. It removes a quarter of clinical capacity for set days, and the generic curriculum needs tailoring to CVO's specific scanner afterwards, but it certifies competence for insurers, regulators and care-quality audits.

Decision: CVO should choose off-the-job certification at the optometry college, followed by supplier-led on-the-job consolidation on the actual machines. Retinal scanning is a clinical governance responsibility — formal certification protects patients, satisfies auditors and strengthens the clinical brand underpinning the boutique's premium positioning. On-the-job training alone is rejected because an equipment demo is not an audit-grade competency record and leaves CVO exposed if a diagnostic error prompts review; the $6,400 fee is easily justified by the $780,000 investment above it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CVO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of CVO.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of CVO with a well-justified decision covering clinical governance, cost and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CVO's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $232,000 ÷ ($55.00 − $26.00) = $232,000 ÷ $29.00 = 8,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 8,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $55.00 − $26.00 = $29.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $29.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CVO's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 8,000-unit break-even with 14,500 patient consultations and eyewear sales shows a margin of safety of 6,500 units (45% of output), comfortably absorbing the extra fixed-cost load of a second branch before it reaches maturity.
2. Contribution data lets CVO model the 57% under-30 contact-lens preference: bundling lenses at a promotional $48 lifts unit volume but cuts contribution to $22.00, so managers can test whether extra lens sales still cover $232,000 of fixed costs.
3. Unit cost data — ($232,000 ÷ 14,500) + $26.00 = $42.00 per unit — lets managers benchmark consultation efficiency, frame-margin leakage in the boutique and lab costs, and renegotiate imported frame terms amid 13.8% material inflation.
4. Labour productivity of 14,500 ÷ 41 = about 354 units per employee lets managers set staffing for the second branch, identify the bottleneck creating 12-day waits, and justify the retinal-scanning certification for the 10 targeted staff.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 8,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $29.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 6,500 units versus 14,500 produced; contact-lens bundle pricing for the 57% under-30 segment; unit-cost benchmarking at $42.00 against 13.8% material inflation; and productivity targets of about 354 units per employee to staff the second branch.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CVO's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has CVO's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 46.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 16.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $720,000 on revenue of $1,600,000 (720 ÷ 1,600 = 45.0%); 2025 gross profit $897,000 on revenue of $1,950,000 (897 ÷ 1,950 = 46.0%). Operating profit rose from $256,000 (256 ÷ 1,600 = 16.0% of revenue) to $351,000 (351 ÷ 1,950 = 18.0% of revenue). With capital employed of $1,280,000 in 2024 and $1,560,000 in 2025, the return on capital moved from 256 ÷ 1,280 = 20.0% to 351 ÷ 1,560 = 22.5%. Revenue grew $350,000 (21.9%) while cost of sales grew $173,000, so the premium designer mix and 18% boutique growth are compounding.

Evaluation: Performance has improved across all three measures, and the 46.0% gross profitability reflects CVO's shift towards designer frames and premium lenses. Interest payable rose from $20,000 to $29,000 as borrowings edged up alongside retained profit, and the retinal-scanning investment will depress near-term efficiency gains during staff certification. Risks: 13.8% imported lens inflation bites directly on a $1,053,000 cost of sales base, the 6.1% minimum wage rise lands in April 2026, and the second boutique's ramp could dilute returns if the launch underperforms.

Conclusion: CVO's financial performance has improved — profitability (45.0% to 46.0%), operating margin (16.0% to 18.0%) and return on capital employed (20.0% to 22.5%). The trajectory is excellent for an independent retailer, but CVO must defend it through supplier renegotiation, tight control of second-branch costs and converting boutique footfall into clinical rebookings before material and wage inflation compress the $29.00 contribution per unit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on whether CVO's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: CVO is piloting recycled acetate frames in its designer range. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CVO of introducing recycled acetate frames.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled acetate frames give CVO an exclusive, eco-conscious designer story that resonates with the 69% of surveyed respondents willing to pay a premium, differentiating the boutique from mass-market chains and reinforcing the premium positioning that lifted frame sales 18% year-on-year. They also attract younger buyers — the 57% under-30s segment — and strengthen local press and influencer coverage ahead of the second branch opening.

Disadvantage: Recycled acetate collections cost more to source and offer fewer style options, raising the $26.00 variable cost and squeezing the $29.00 contribution per unit unless premium prices hold. Small-batch supply also risks stockouts of popular sizes and stranded inventory if trends shift, increasing working capital pressure at exactly the moment CVO is funding a $780,000 second branch and retinal-scanning suite.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CVO's boutique expansion, research data and cost base.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.8% rise in imported lens materials will affect CVO. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): Because the second branch is funded mainly by the $480,000 share issue and $300,000 retained profit, CVO's exposure is limited — mainly its overdraft and any residual borrowing, costing perhaps under $5,000 a year — plus softer consumer confidence for discretionary designer purchases. The $5.25% rate also strengthens the case for share-funded expansion over debt, which CVO has already executed effectively.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $13.16): CVO's retail, reception and frame-styling teams include many near-minimum-wage roles. On 24 eligible staff averaging 1,900 hours, the current wage bill is about 24 x $12.40 x 1,900 = $565,000; a 6.1% rise adds roughly $34,500 a year, concentrated on opening hours and the new boutique's launch staffing.

Imported lens material inflation (13.8%): Imported lenses and frames are the largest cost of sales component — on a $1,053,000 cost of sales base, the imported share is roughly $370,000; a 13.8% rise adds about $51,000 a year, directly eroding the $29.00 contribution unless CVO renegotiates with suppliers, shifts lens mix towards higher-margin boutique packages or adjusts retail prices modestly.

Conclusion: The 13.8% imported lens material inflation will have the greatest impact. It adds roughly $51,000 a year against about $34,500 of extra wages and under $5,000 of interest, and it attacks every one of the 14,500 units CVO sells while supply chains remain currency-exposed. CVO should renegotiate supplier contracts, hedge currency where practical, and lean into the premium designer mix (already 18% up) to absorb the rise — the share-issue financing means CVO can weather this without additional borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CVO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CVO's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CVO with a well-justified judgment that imported lens inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
